title: Spot the broken filter
idea: TOOL: common filter mistakes — appending outside the if, forgetting the empty list, testing the wrong thing. Read and predict.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show? (Look closely at the indentation.)

nums = [4, 9, 2, 7]
kept = []
for n in nums:
    if n > 5:
        pass
    kept.append(n)
print(kept)
exercises.explanation: The append is lined up with the if, not inside it, so EVERY item is kept. The filter does nothing — a classic indentation bug.

exercises.prompt: A learner wants to keep numbers above 5 but gets the whole list back. The append line is not indented under the if. What is the fix?
options: Indent the append so it sits inside the if
exercises.explanation: Only items that pass should be appended, so the append must be indented inside the if. Indentation decides what the if controls.

exercises.prompt: Putting the append inside the if is what makes a filter keep only SOME items instead of all of them.
exercises.explanation: The if is the gate. Appending inside it means only passers get through; appending outside keeps everything.

options: kept was never created with kept = [] before the loop
append cannot be used in a loop
exercises.explanation: You can't append into a list that doesn't exist yet. The line kept = [] must come before the loop.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show?

nums = [3, 6, 9]
kept = []
for n in nums:
    if n > 5:
        kept.append(n)
print(kept)
exercises.explanation: This one is correct: 6 and 9 pass n > 5, so kept is [6, 9]. Always worth reading a working one to compare against the broken ones.

exercises.prompt: A filter is supposed to keep EVEN numbers but keeps odd ones instead. The test reads if n % 2 == 1. What is wrong?
options: n % 2 == 1 is the ODD test; even should be n % 2 == 0
You cannot use % in a filter
exercises.explanation: Remainder 1 means odd. For even, the remainder must be 0, so the test should be n % 2 == 0. The wrong test keeps the wrong items.

exercises.prompt: If a filter returns an empty list, that always means the code is broken.
exercises.explanation: Not always! If no item passes the test, an empty list is the correct, honest answer. Check your data before assuming a bug.

exercises.prompt:
What will this show?

nums = [10, 20, 30]
kept = []
for n in nums:
    if n > 100:
        kept.append(n)
print(kept)
exercises.explanation: Nothing is above 100, so nothing is appended. The kept list stays empty — a correct result, not an error.

exercises.prompt: A filter accidentally resets kept = [] INSIDE the loop, before each test. What happens?
options: The kept list is wiped every pass, so it ends holding at most the last match
exercises.explanation: Resetting the list each pass throws away everything collected so far. The empty-list line belongs BEFORE the loop, once.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines into a correct filter for numbers above 5.
exercises.explanation: List, empty kept list before the loop, loop, test, append INSIDE the if, then print. Getting this order right avoids every bug above.
